visual_behaviour.never: Do not show the result while a prediction is still open, and never draw a cancelled pair as an empty space. An empty space is the deletion misconception rendered.
visual_behaviour.scene: A horizontal fraction bar with factor blocks in a row above it and a row below. An uncancelled block takes the primary accent; a cancelled pair greys and each of its two blocks is redrawn carrying a 1. Leftovers below the bar keep the second accent so the fraction form is visible.
visual_behaviour.layout: The bar sits across the middle of the main panel with both rows centred on it and the value readout directly beneath. On a 390 px frame the rows wrap in pairs so a factor and its partner stay vertically aligned.
readouts: m and n, always on screen
How many pairs have been cancelled and how many factors survive on each side, live
The value, held on screen through every cancel so it can be seen not to move
animations: Cancel: the two blocks fade to grey together over 180 ms and each flips to a 1, so the pair is seen becoming one rather than vanishing.
Value hold: the value readout pulses once but does not change when a pair cancels, which is the invariant made watchable.
Full cancel: when the last pair goes, the bar is left holding 1 over 1 and pauses there for the question before anything is written.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Block size is derived from the panel width and the larger of m and n so every base glyph stays at least 16 px and each block keeps a 44 px tap target; above 8 blocks a row wraps rather than shrinking.

teaching_sequence.rationale: A cancelled pair has to be seen becoming a 1 before m minus n is written, or cancelling is learnt as crossing out and the fully cancelled case gets read as zero

tool_config.image_prompts_note: Empty by design. This mount is a mechanism, not a depiction, and the standard mandates hand-built inline SVG with no external asset dependency, so no depictive picture is declared.
mathematical_facts: a to the m over a to the n is a to the m minus n
A matched pair divides to 1, so cancelling changes the writing and never the value
When m equals n every factor pairs off and the value is 1, which is not nothing
When n is greater than m the leftovers stay below the bar, which is where a negative exponent begins

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.
question_integration.parse_rule: Read the base and both exponents out of the question text (the numerator power and the denominator power). Set m and n from them without cancelling anything. teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the pairing visible before any arithmetic is done. Five 3s stand above the bar and two below, nothing cancelled, and the class is asked OUT LOUD how many threes will be left. The value 27 is already on screen, which is deliberate: it is the number the rest of the demonstration will show refusing to move.

Beat 2 is the argument in one motion. Two pairs cancel, each pair greying together and each block flipping to a 1, and the value read-out is recomputed from the base and the counts — so it cannot move, and the class watches it not move. Point at the read-out before you say anything about it.

Beat 3 carries the idea to its edge. The counts are set equal, every pair cancels, and the bar is left holding 1 over 1. Ask what that is worth before reading the strip: the answer 1 has to be produced by argument, because the whole misconception this tool exists to break is that a fully cancelled fraction is worth nothing.
media.generation_prompt: Quotient Law Deriver: numerator factors above a bar and denominator factors below it, where a tapped pair greys out together and what is left is read off as a single power
media.instructions_for_student: Tap a factor above the bar, then a factor below it, and watch the pair cancel. Neither block disappears: each is struck through and drawn as a 1, because 3 over 3 is 1 and multiplying by 1 changes nothing. Keep an eye on the value while you cancel — it never moves. When every pair has gone the bar is left holding 1 over 1, which is 1, and when the row below is the longer one the leftovers stay below the bar and the answer is an exact fraction.

media.title: Zero Exponent Staircase
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash 'Power Play' — the zero exponent, met immediately after the quotient law and the fully cancelled fraction. The class has already seen a power as a count of factors and aᵐ ÷ aᵐ = 1; what it has not seen is the descending table carried one row further. This tool sits on the Justify beat: the pattern is watched arriving at the same place from above, so a⁰ = 1 is FORCED rather than announced. Negative exponents are the next tool and the staircase deliberately hands over to it rather than stopping at 1.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the staircase that explains it.
whatYouLearned: Each step down the staircase divides by the base, because it removes one factor
a to the 0 is 1 for every base other than zero
The reason never mentions the base, which is why one argument settles them all

overview.goal: The student continues a descending pattern to justify the value of a power with exponent zero, and says why the answer is one for any non zero base.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground carrying a staircase of value cards descending to the right, each pair of steps joined by a labelled dividing arrow. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class is split between a power with exponent zero being zero and being the base itself, and the dividing staircase is asked where the next step lands.
overview.concept: Each step down the staircase divides by the base, because dropping the exponent by one removes one factor. Continuing that from a to the 1, which is a, gives a divided by a, which is 1. So a to the 0 is 1 for every non zero base. Nothing about the base enters the argument, which is why the answer does not depend on it.
overview.purpose: The student continues a descending pattern to justify the value of a power with exponent zero, and says why the answer is one for any non zero base.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Staircase fills the main panel with the exponent printed beside each step and the base selector beneath. On a 390 px frame the top steps scroll out of view while the last three and the empty slot stay pinned, because the bottom is where the argument is. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not write the value of the zero exponent step while a prediction is still open, and never present it as a stated rule. The dividing arrow IS the justification.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The staircase is built by one rule: each step is the previous divided by the base. That rule is not a convention, it is what removing a factor does. Applying it to the step a to the 1, whose value is a, gives a over a, and any non zero number divided by itself is 1. Because the argument never mentions which number a is, it settles every base at once. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): The landing at 1 does not depend on the values shrinking, so a flat staircase is not a broken one. Breaks: Believing the landing on 1 comes from the values getting smaller, so a staircase that never shrinks is read as failing. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): The rule a to the 0 is 1 holds for every base except 0, and the staircase shows exactly why. Breaks: Believing a to the 0 is 1 for absolutely every base, base 0 included. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): The landing is forced by the dividing rule, not by the size of the base. Breaks: Believing a to the 0 is a separate fact that has to be memorised for each base. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The exponent 0 is a step on the way down, not the bottom of the staircase. Breaks: Believing the pattern ends at the exponent 0 because the whole numbers have run out. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): A zero exponent means no factors are multiplied, and the product of no factors is 1, never 0. Breaks: 2 to the power 0 taken as 0, on the reading that a zero exponent removes the number.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the base 2 staircase reading 16, 8, 4, 2 with the next slot empty, and ask the class to say out loud what comes next and what the zero exponent step will be. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Targets base 2 with four steps shown. Never drop the next step before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Drop the next step so its dividing arrow draws itself first and the value it forces lands beside the committed guess. Point at the arrow label and then at the bottom step. Targets base 2 at the exponent zero. Read the landed value from getState().truth. Call 3. Rebuild the staircase at base 5 and then at base 10, and before base 7 is drawn ask the class whether the landing will be the same. Targets base 5, base 10 and then base 7. Read each landing from the tool's own readout, never from this plan.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Removing one factor from a power is exactly dividing by the base once
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Every arrow on the staircase carries the same instruction, divide by the base
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The staircase is built by one rule, so the last step is not a special case that needs its own rule

observationsAndConclusions.why: The final step is the base divided by itself, and any number other than zero divided by itself is 1
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Changing the base rewrites every card but the bottom card still reads 1
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The argument settles every base at once, which is why the answer does not depend on the base

observationsAndConclusions.why: The dividing step would be a division by zero, so the staircase cannot be built at all
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Base zero is refused rather than drawn
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The one base excluded is excluded for a reason that is on the arrow, not by decree

media.description: A staircase of value cards descends to the right, one card per exponent, each card carrying NCERT's two columns — the index form beside its value, so the card reads 2³ = 8 rather than a bare 8 — and each pair of cards joined by an arrow whose pill states the rule as ÷ the base. Every column of the scene shares ONE exponent axis, so two staircases of different heights land on the SAME row and the claim that the base does not move the landing is true in the drawing rather than asserted beside it. The base can be rebuilt from 0 to 10: at base 1 the staircase is flat and still lands on 1, and at base 0 the machinery visibly jams at the arrow — a ÷ 0 pill drawn above a dashed slot that reads no value — instead of the base being greyed out on a selector. Free Play docks an empty step under the last one and checks a typed value against the previous value divided by the base rather than against a stored fact, refusing a wrong entry by highlighting the arrow and never by stating the answer, and the descent carries on past the exponent 0 into 1/3 and 1/9 drawn as real stacked fractions. Practice renders the scene each bank question describes — the stated staircase, the product's other factor, the four powers to be ordered — masks only the quantity the item asks for until the check, and grades every answer against the value the drawn scene itself computes.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the base from its own numbers, shows the question, then reveals the staircase, the dividing arrow and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the staircase 16, 8, 4, 2 and the next step EMPTY, and asks what comes next and what 2 to the 0 will be. Beat 2 drops the next step into place and the halving arrow forces the value 1. Beat 3 changes the base to 5 and then to 10, and the class is asked whether the answer would still be one for base 7 before base 7 is shown. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setBase, dropStep and say.

concept.notation: Write a to the 0. The exponent 0 means no factors are multiplied, and the product of no factors is 1.
concept.statement: Each step down the staircase divides by the base, because dropping the exponent by one removes one factor. Continuing that from a to the 1, which is a, gives a divided by a, which is 1. So a to the 0 is 1 for every non zero base. Nothing about the base enters the argument, which is why the answer does not depend on it.
prerequisites: a power as a count of factors
the quotient law and a fully cancelled fraction
misconceptions: 2 to the 0 taken as 0, on the reading that a zero exponent removes the number.
2 to the 0 taken as 2, on the reading that a zero exponent does nothing at all.
concept.why_it_is_true: The staircase is built by one rule: each step is the previous divided by the base. That rule is not a convention, it is what removing a factor does. Applying it to the step a to the 1, whose value is a, gives a over a, and any non zero number divided by itself is 1. Because the argument never mentions which number a is, it settles every base at once.
worked_numbers: Base 2: 16, 8, 4, 2, then 1, so 2 to the 0 is 1.
Base 5: 625, 125, 25, 5, then 1, so the same landing from a different height.
Base 10: 1000, 100, 10, then 1, which is the step that makes the place value columns line up.

extra: A length halved again and again until the halvings run out

A photocopy of a photocopy traced back to the original page
A savings amount stepped back year by year to the day it was deposited

answer_key.worked: a to the 0 is 1 for every non zero base, because each step down divides by the base and a divided by a is 1.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn staircase: the value of the zero exponent step, the value of a product containing one, or whether a stated reason appeals to the pattern rather than to a rule.
answer_key.precision: Exact integer arithmetic throughout, with BigInt above 2 to the 53. Each step is computed as the previous divided exactly by the base, never as a rounded quotient.
answer_key.ground_truth: step(a, k) = a to the k, computed exactly. nextStep(v, a) = v / a as an exact division, defined only when a is non zero. value(a, 0) = 1 for every a not equal to 0. 0 to the 0 is refused as undefined here.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

Every arrow on the staircase carries the same instruction — ÷ the base — and the bottom card is simply what that instruction produces at the exponent 0. Ask the class out loud what comes after 16, 8, 4, 2 before you read the bottom card, then point at the arrow rather than at the value: the arrow is the justification, and naming a⁰ = 1 as a rule at this beat throws the argument away.

Beat 2 is the whole proof in one row of the picture. The value at the exponent 1 is the base itself, so the last step is the base divided by itself — and the second strip line shows the same thing arriving from the quotient law, 2³ ÷ 2³ = 2⁰, which the class met last lesson. Two routes, one landing.

Beat 3 is where the generalisation is earned rather than stated. Every value on the screen changes as the base moves and the bottom row does not, because the argument never named which number the base was. Ask whether base 7 would land anywhere else BEFORE calling setBase(7), so the class commits and the tool settles it.

media.title: Walking the Power Line Backwards
media.context: This hook opens the topic on dividing powers, the zero exponent and negative exponents. Students know the multiplication laws. The film must not give the value at zero and must not state what a negative exponent means.
media.description: You already climb a power line by multiplying by the base at every step, so what happens when you turn round and walk back down? Divide again and again and the exponents shrink, until you land on zero and then step past it into negative territory.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Divide powers of the same base, and interpret the zero and negative exponents that follow. Key teaching points: 1) Dividing powers of the same base subtracts the exponents. 2) Continuing the pattern past one gives an exponent of zero. 3) Any non zero base to the power zero equals one. 4) A negative exponent gives the reciprocal of the positive power. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often say a base to the power zero is zero. 2) Students often think a negative exponent makes a negative number. Pause points: 0:24, at the end of past zero: ask what value belongs at an exponent of zero. 0:24, just before the open question: ask what the class expects at minus one. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what dividing by the base does to the exponent. After viewing, ask what two to the power minus six might be.

media.title: Division Rule, n^a ÷ n^b = n^(a, b)
media.context: Plays on M3.S4.T4.C38, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: A 150-second animated whiteboard walkthrough showing a 16-unit line being halved repeatedly. Scene 1: 16 = 2⁴ units long. Halving once: 16 ÷ 2 = 8 = 2³, with the cancelled 2 highlighted in Orange. Scene 2: halving again gives 4 = 2² (subtract 2 from the exponent). Scene 3: halving three times gives 2 = 2¹, with the visible cancellation (2 × 2 × 2 × 2) / (2 × 2 × 2). Scene 4 generalises to n^a ÷ n^b = n^(a−b). Scene 5 computes 2¹⁰⁰ ÷ 2²⁵ = 2⁷⁵ in one step.
media.teaching_notes: Play this video AFTER the student has read the textbook's halving-line setup. Pause at 45s and ask 'What would the length be after halving twice more?', this is the attempt-before-reveal moment; expect the answer 4 (after one more halve) or 2 (after two more). After the boxed rule appears, ask 'How is this rule different from Law 1 (the product rule)? When do we add exponents and when do we subtract?' to consolidate the operation pairing. End-of-video question: 'Compute 3⁸ ÷ 3² using the rule, and verify by expanding both sides.'.

media.description: A 130-second animated whiteboard walkthrough deriving n⁰ = 1. topics.summary: Halving a power line drives the exponent down: dividing powers of one base subtracts the exponents, reaching exponent 0 gives a length of 1, and stepping into negative exponents gives reciprocals, so 2 to the 0 is 1 and 2 to the -1 is one half.

content.text: When two powers share a base, dividing them cancels matching factors. 2 to the 8 divided by 2 to the 3 has eight 2s on top and three 2s on the bottom; three pairs cancel, leaving five 2s, so the answer is 2 to the 5. The exponent is a count of factors, so you subtract the counts: 8 - 3 = 5. In general, a to the m divided by a to the n = a to the (m - n), as long as the base is not 0.

content.text: What does an exponent of 0 mean? Divide any power by an equal power, like 2 to the 3 divided by 2 to the 3. All the factors cancel, so the answer is 1. By the subtract rule the same division is 2 to the (3 - 3) = 2 to the 0. So 2 to the 0 must be 1. This works for any base that is not 0: n to the 0 = 1. On the power line, stepping down to the exponent 0 lands on a length of 1, not 0.

content.text: What lies to the left of the exponent 0 on the power line? Each step left divides by the base again, so past length 1 the lengths become fractions. 2 to the -1 is half of 1, which is 1/2; 2 to the -6 is 1 over 2 to the 6, which is 1/64. A negative exponent means one over the positive power: n to the -a = 1 over n to the a. The minus sign counts divisions; it never makes the number negative, so 2 to the -1 = 1/2, not -2.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what happens to the factors when two powers of the same base are divided through observation and reasoning, and determine that each factor on the bottom cancels one on top, so the exponents subtract and 2 to the 8 divided by 2 to the 3 is 2 to the 5. They will explain that the counts of factors are subtracted and not divided, and that this holds for any base that is not 0.
Examine the worked examples of dividing powers of the same base, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving dividing powers of the same base, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what an exponent of 0 means through observation and reasoning, and determine that any power divided by an equal power leaves 1, so by the subtract rule that reaches exponent 0 and 2 to the 0 must be 1. They will explain that this holds for every base that is not 0, so stepping down to exponent 0 lands on a length of 1 and never on 0.
Examine the worked examples of the zero exponent, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving the zero exponent, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what lies to the left of exponent 0 through observation and reasoning, and determine that each step left divides by the base again, so a negative exponent means one over the matching positive power and 2 to the negative 1 is one half. They will explain that the minus sign counts divisions and never changes the sign of the number, so 2 to the negative 1 is one half and not negative 2.

media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: A place value chart runs across the picture with columns headed by their powers, 10 to the 3, 10 to the 2, 10 to the 1 and 10 to the 0, each with its plain value beneath as 1000, 100, 10 and 1. The digits 3, 7, 2 and 8 sit one per column, each with a product strip beneath reading its digit times its power: 3 times 10 to the 3, 7 times 10 to the 2, 2 times 10 to the 1 and 8 times 10 to the 0. An expanded form card gathers them with plus signs, and a value check strip reads '3000 + 700 + 20 + 8 = 3728'. A note at the side reads that after a decimal point the places keep shrinking by ten, so they use negative exponents. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: 10 to the 3; 10 to the 2; 10 to the 1; 10 to the 0; 1000; 100; 10; 1; 3; 7; 2; 8; 3000 + 700 + 20 + 8 = 3728; after the point the exponents go negative.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The columns must be headed 10 to the 3, 10 to the 2, 10 to the 1 and 10 to the 0, with plain values 1000, 100, 10 and 1.
The digits 3, 7, 2 and 8 must sit in those columns in order.
The expanded form must total 3728.
The ones column must be headed 10 to the 0.
The note must state that places after the point use negative exponents.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Power Comparison Duel
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Exponents and Powers, the Powers of Ten segment - place value, standard form and comparison. This closes the chapter: the product law, the power of a power law, a to the power 0 and negative exponents have all been met, so the duel is where the student chooses which law applies rather than being told. It rehearses the 1 mark 'which is larger' board reading and the 2 mark rewrite item directly, and it is the mount that breaks the two comparison misconceptions the chapter names.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's pick, the student's reason, the valid reasons, and both values.

overview.goal: The student decides which of two powers is larger and justifies the choice by rewriting to a common base or exponent rather than by guessing.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground with two power cards dealt side by side, their value panels blank, and a list of reasons beneath them. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class backs the card with the bigger base without computing either value, and both cards stay face down until a reason is given.
overview.concept: Two powers can be compared without full evaluation by putting them on a common footing. With the same base, the larger exponent wins. With the same exponent, the larger base wins. Otherwise one card must be rewritten so that a base or an exponent is shared, and only then does a comparison follow. A bigger base alone and a bigger exponent alone decide nothing.
overview.purpose: The student decides which of two powers is larger and justifies the choice by rewriting to a common base or exponent rather than by guessing.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Cards fill the upper main panel side by side, reason list directly beneath, scoreboard to the right on a wide frame and collapsed to a strip under the reasons on a 390 px frame. Every reason row keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not reveal either value before the reason is submitted, and never display or reward elapsed time. A revealed value turns the duel into arithmetic and a timer turns it into a race.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Powers grow by multiplication, so the two numbers in a card interact rather than competing separately. Rewriting to a common base or a common exponent makes one of them cancel out of the decision, and what is left is a comparison of single numbers, which can be settled by ordinary size. Without such a rewrite, neither number in the card is by itself evidence about the value. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.summary: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item deals its own pair, shows the question, then reveals the reason, the rewrite and both values together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A bigger base is not by itself evidence about the value of a card. Breaks: Comparing by the bigger base alone, so 5 to the power 3 is taken as the larger card. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Equal is a legitimate outcome, because two different writings can name one value. Breaks: Believing a duel must always have a winner, so two powers are never allowed to coincide. ML3 (Medium, Conceptual): Each shortcut needs a shared field, and without one neither number in a card is evidence. Breaks: Comparing by the bigger exponent alone, without checking whether the bases are comparable. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): Some pairs have no common footing, and saying so is the method rather than a failure. Breaks: Believing every pair can be rewritten onto a common base, so a rewrite is invented. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): A correct pick with an invalid reason is only partly right, because the reason is what is graded. Breaks: Treating a correct answer as proof that the method behind it was sound.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 deals 2 to the 10 against 10 to the 3 with both values HIDDEN and asks which is larger and how the class knows. Beat 2 takes the committed reason and applies it, rewriting both cards onto a common footing. Beat 3 reveals both values, so the reason is seen to have decided the duel before the arithmetic did. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with dealPair, chooseReason, revealValues and say.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open with two cards dealt, both value panels blank and no reason chosen, and ask the class to say out loud which is larger and how they know. Commit the class pick and reason on the prediction pad. Targets the pair 2 to the power 10 against 10 cubed. Never reveal either value at this call. Call 2. Apply the committed reason so one card rewrites and the shared base or exponent lights up. Point at the rewritten card and then at the shared field. Targets the rewrite onto a common base. Say what the comparison has been reduced to, and read the rewritten form from the tool's own readout. Call 3. Reveal both values at once and set them beside the reason that was given. Targets both value panels. Read both values from getState().truth, never from this plan, and say whether the reason had settled the duel before the arithmetic was done.

hunts: BASE TRAP: find three pairs where the card with the smaller base wins.
DEAD HEAT: deal pairs until you find two cards of exactly equal value, and say how you knew.
ONE REASON ONLY: settle four duels without ever using the same reason twice.
NO REWRITE: find a pair that no rewrite settles, and say what you used instead.

observationsAndConclusions.why: If one landed first it would be read first, and the duel would be decided by arithmetic rather than by the reason
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Both value panels fill at exactly the same instant
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A comparison is a piece of reasoning, and the values are only its confirmation

observationsAndConclusions.why: Once a base is common, the two values differ only in their exponents, and single numbers can be ordered by size
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Rewriting one card so a base is shared makes the other number drop out of the decision
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The point of a rewrite is to remove one of the two numbers from the argument

observationsAndConclusions.why: The base and the exponent interact by multiplication, so neither one alone is evidence about the value
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A card with the bigger base can hold the smaller value
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Comparing on one number of a power is a habit that has to be given up, not adjusted

media.description: Two power cards are dealt side by side on a plain working ground, each showing a base with a raised exponent in large type and a value panel beneath it. Under the pair run two magnitude bars that start from ONE origin and use ONE unit, so their lengths are exactly proportional to the two values - which is why 2 to the power 10 and 10 to the power 3 draw as two bars a hair apart rather than as a rout. Concept walks three teaching beats: the pair whose bigger base loses by 24, the pair that rewrites onto one base until both cards read the same glyphs, and the pair that no rewrite reaches. Learn stages the five reviewed checkpoints, each opening with its answer and both values already on screen and taking no input at all. Practice serves six questions drawn from a thirty item pool on a difficulty ladder, masking both value panels until the attempt is in, then naming the reasons that genuinely settle that pair. Free Play is the duel itself: tap the card you believe is larger, choose a reason from the five, watch a valid rewrite transform a card with the shared field lighting up, and only then reveal both values - which fill at the same instant so neither is read first. A scoreboard records which reasons have been used. No elapsed time is displayed anywhere and none is scored.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item deals its own pair, shows the question, then reveals the reason, the rewrite and both values together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 deals 2 to the 10 against 10 to the 3 with both values HIDDEN and asks which is larger and how the class knows. Beat 2 takes the committed reason and applies it, rewriting both cards onto a common footing. Beat 3 reveals both values, so the reason is seen to have decided the duel before the arithmetic did. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with dealPair, chooseReason, revealValues and say.

concept.notation: A card reads a to the n. Comparing cards means deciding which value is larger without necessarily computing either one.
concept.statement: Two powers can be compared without full evaluation by putting them on a common footing. With the same base, the larger exponent wins. With the same exponent, the larger base wins. Otherwise one card must be rewritten so that a base or an exponent is shared, and only then does a comparison follow. A bigger base alone and a bigger exponent alone decide nothing.
prerequisites: the product law and the power of a power law
powers of ten and orders of magnitude
misconceptions: Comparing by the bigger base alone, so 10 to the 3 is taken as larger than 2 to the 10.
Comparing by the bigger exponent alone, without checking whether the bases are comparable.
concept.why_it_is_true: Powers grow by multiplication, so the two numbers in a card interact rather than competing separately. Rewriting to a common base or a common exponent makes one of them cancel out of the decision, and what is left is a comparison of single numbers, which can be settled by ordinary size. Without such a rewrite, neither number in the card is by itself evidence about the value.
worked_numbers: 2 to the 10 is 1024 and 10 to the 3 is 1000, so the smaller base wins, which the bigger base reading gets exactly backwards.
2 to the 8 against 4 to the 4: rewriting 4 as 2 squared gives 2 to the 8 on both sides, so they are equal.
3 times 10 to the 8 against 9 times 10 to the 7: a whole decade separates them, so the exponent settles it before the coefficient is looked at.

extra: Two savings plans, one doubling for ten years and one growing tenfold for three
Two rumours, one told to two people a day and one told to ten people every third day
Two stacks of folded paper, folded different numbers of times from different starting thicknesses
Two colonies, one splitting in two every hour and one tripling every two hours
Two prize schemes, one paying a power of 3 and one a power of 9
Two file sizes written as powers of 2 and compared without expanding them
textbook: Two powers of ten compared by their exponents alone
A power of 2 compared with a power of ten of similar size
Two quantities in standard form compared exponent first
A power rewritten on a common base so two expressions can be set against each other

answer_key.worked: Compare the exponent first when the bases match and the base first when the exponents match; otherwise rewrite one card until something is shared, and only then decide.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the dealt pair: which card is larger by exact BigInt comparison, and whether the chosen reason is in the item's set of valid reason tags.
answer_key.precision: Both values are held as BigInt strings so a card such as 2 to the 40 compares exactly. No comparison is ever made on a float and no point is ever awarded for response time.
answer_key.ground_truth: value(a, n) = BigInt exponentiation. larger(cardA, cardB) = BigInt comparison of the two values, or 'equal'. validReasons(pair) = the tags that genuinely settle this pair, computed from whether the bases match, the exponents match, or a rewrite exists.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Equal is an allowed pick and the tool says so. Forcing a larger card would teach that two powers can never coincide, which 2 to the 8 against 4 to the 4 immediately disproves.

edge_cases.case: A correct pick with an invalid reason
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Scored as partially correct and a hint is triggered. The reason is the graded object, so a lucky pick cannot score full.

edge_cases.case: A pair where no rewrite exists
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Estimation is the only route and the tool says so, offering the bounding decade as the valid reason rather than pretending a rewrite is available.
Comparison is BigInt so 2 to the 40 style cards do not overflow, and the revealed values are printed in full rather than in exponential notation.

edge_cases.case: A student trying to reveal before reasoning
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Blocked. Values are never revealed before the reason is submitted, because the whole design is to make the reason precede the arithmetic.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]

terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.

steps: The bases differ and the exponents differ, so neither number alone decides.

5 to the power 3 is 125.
